segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Sullivan High School in Chicago is a school where communication isn't the easiest in normal times. Kids constantly have to pass their phones back and forth with Google Translate so they can understand each other.

segments.speaker: Elly Fishman
segments.text: Over half the kids are immigrants or refugees. They come from close to 40 different countries. They speak over 35 different languages.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's Elly Fishman, a reporter who spent over three years there and wrote a book about the school called Refugee High. She returned there with one of our producers at the beginning of this school year and was there on the second day of school.

segments.speaker: Elly Fishman
segments.text: Kids are really nervous. They're not native English speakers. They don't know each other yet. So they're sitting among a bunch of strangers at this point. So there's a lot of anxiety and nerves.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Sullivan High School is organized to make them feel at home. Each step at the staircase by the main entrance says welcome in a different language, private spaces for Muslim students to pray, shelves full of winter coats and backpacks for students who arrive with none, special curriculum and services tailored to them. This year, though, was the first time students were back in person since the pandemic, which posed some special challenges.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Like, for instance, English teacher Annmarie Handley was going around the room student by student doing one of the most pedestrian beginning of school tasks-- filling out the seating chart with the basics. What country are they from? What do they speak besides English?

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: Abdal? What languages do you speak?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I speak Arabic.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: What languages do you speak, sir?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK. Now, you heard that student perfectly, because our producer was standing right next to him with a microphone just inches from his face. But that long pause, the fact that Ms. Handley asked him the question a second time, that's going to make a lot more sense if I just play you the sound from the microphone that was pinned to Ms. Handley's lapel. This is how she heard that interaction, more or less.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: Abdal? What languages do you speak? What languages do you speak, sir?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. She didn't hear him at all. Because she's way up at the front of the room stuck there typing into a computer. And there's an air purifier that they put in for COVID humming towards the back of the room. And there's an air conditioner running that's in the window just to her right. And most important, everybody is in a mask, muffling the students' voices, and making it so she cannot see anybody's mouth move.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: Now, you can see how much I normally read lips.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She continues her questions.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: And what country were you born in?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Egypt.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: Where?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Egypt.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: Asia? What part of Asia?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No, Egypt.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: Egypt. Cool.

segments.speaker: Elly Fishman
segments.text: So she keeps going around the room. And this keeps happening.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Again, reporter Elly Fishman.

segments.speaker: Elly Fishman
segments.text: It seemed to me, having spent a couple of years in the school before COVID, that it was just exponentially harder. And there was so much more miscommunication.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: All right. And then we have Claude. What languages do you speak?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: What say?

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: What languages do you speak?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Kinyarwanda. Kinyarwanda.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: And what country were you born in?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Congo.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: Rwanda.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I said Congo.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: One more, table.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Dang.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: Huh?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I said Congo.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: Congo.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: Oh my gosh. I'm so sorry. I thought you said Rwanda. I will fix it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's painful to listen to-- hearing these students give the teacher exactly what she's asking for. And she can't tell. Everybody is trying to connect. And they are not connecting. In the recording, you can hear Ms. Handley try to manage this awkwardness, save the students from the embarrassment, turn it all on herself.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: Sorry. It's the air conditioner. It's not you guys. Your English is good. It's just this is right in my ear. And it's killing me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When I reached Ms. Handley, she said, it is a lot harder to conduct this class without being able to see the kids' mouths. But for her, it really just feels like one more thing to deal with.

segments.speaker: Annmarie Handley
segments.text: I think I worry more that the kid is getting frustrated, because especially at the beginning of the year, I need them to know that I'm listening and they can trust me. And I don't want them to feel as though I'm not listening or I don't care.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She says in the months since then, it's gotten a lot easier to communicate. The air conditioning is off. And more important, everybody is more comfortable with each other and with her, which means they're more comfortable speaking up, projecting, making themselves heard through the mask.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Communication is delicate. And if you don't get it right, it could be disastrous. They got through it here in Ms. Handley's class. But in our other stories today, it does not go so well. Like in one story, the future of democracy is at stake. In another, a mom tries to say something important to her own daughter so ineffectively.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Also, Amelia Bedelia-- remember her-- who hears, but never understands. Where is she today? Here. From WBEZ Chicago, this is This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, Until The Cows Come Home. So this first story is about a man trying to communicate a thing, a very particular thing-- that the 2020 election in the state of Michigan was not stolen, that Joe Biden won. This is not an outcome this man is particularly happy about. He's a Republican, a state senator. But he says, this is the truth.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The man's name is Ed McBroom. He chaired the official state committee that looked into all the claims of election fraud in Michigan. In the end, they wrote a report concluding that there was, quote, "no evidence of widespread or systematic fraud."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Lots of his fellow Republicans do not accept this conclusion. And they are not shy about telling him that when they run into him. So Ed has been on a kind of personal campaign to talk to anybody who doubts him, as long as they want, in the hopes of being able to give them the facts they need to reach the same conclusion that he did. Our senior editor David Kestenbaum wondered if he was persuading anybody, and a few months ago went up to spend a day with Ed at the Upper Peninsula State Fair.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Ed promised, from out in the open for five minutes with my cows, somebody will come up and talk about the election. Here's David.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I met Ed in the dairy barn at the state fair with his cows and his kids. That's kind of how he's known, the state senator with the cows and kids.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Helen, Melody, Eddie, Carl, Esther--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: These are the kids, not the cows. There are more.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Brita, Royal, Odell, Oriana, Kenny-Jack, Edith, Magnus, and Sayla. So there's 13 of them.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: You want to say a word about what that life is like? If you had to pick one word.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: One word-- I think I'm going to say blessed, I guess. Blessed or hard-- blessed or hard.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Five of the kids are Ed's. The other eight were his brother's, who died three years ago and lived next door. So the families were always kind of one unit.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: There's one photo I saw on Ed's Facebook page of a kid who had put together some delightfully crazy outfit. But the thing that stood out to me was the stuff in the background of the photo, total chaos in the kitchen behind her. Ed's a farmer, a parent, and a state senator. He says sometimes, it's a bit much to handle.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I was interested in Ed, because honestly, it's alarming to me all the people who still believe the election was stolen. In one poll, a third of Americans and most Republicans. It's bad enough that we as a country seem completely divided on everything-- the climate, vaccines, immigration. But somehow, this idea that so many people look at the official election results certified by the states-- the method we have for settling all these disputes-- and say, that's a lie. That feels particularly unsettling.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And so here was Ed, this guy in the trenches, arguing for the facts in a way that few people are. I wanted to see how that was going and what the conversations were like. Ed ventures out of the dairy barn, where his cows are, past the fair games and the rides, to this indoor area where various vendors are set up, and where the Republican Party has a table.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Hello, ma'am. Hi.

segments.speaker: Donna
segments.text: Hi. I was at Cityfest last week--

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: People stop by who know him to catch up. A woman from the Gideon's Bible table across the way, comes over to say that they've been praying for him. And then this man and a woman come over. The first thing she says is, why aren't you having a full forensic audit?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Forensic audit is the battle cry for people who want some external group to look at the ballots and everything, which for the record, have already been through a state-led, bipartisan audit in Michigan.

segments.speaker: Donna
segments.text: So why aren't you having a full forensic audit?

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: You need one, badly. Those two vans that went in the FTC center in the middle of the night with nobody watching except the cameras-- and I saw it on Gateway Pundit. I know they went in there. And the little black car phone--

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Well, nobody's denying that the vans came. It's just that we know what was in them--

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Bull--

segments.speaker: Donna
segments.text: Dan, stop.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Well, I mean, the facts are--

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: You do not know--

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Well, sure we do.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Did you see every ballot that was in there and see that it was folded, if it was mail-in? Did you see that it was signed?

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: So listen--

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Did you check any of this?

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: So listen to the explanation, though. I mean, because--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Ed's approach to these conversations is to answer whatever questions people have in detail, however long it takes, which is premised on an idea that I hope is true, but I kind of fear isn't. Basically, if you calmly present people with facts, they'll consider them.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The thing the man is asking Ed about is something that got a lot of attention online, a video of a van arriving at the convention center in Detroit after 3:00 in the morning with a bunch of ballots. Seemed suspicious to them.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Ed lays out what his committee found. Those were ballots that had been placed in drop boxes, which he points out he's not a fan of drop boxes. But he says he looked into it. And the ballots were just going through the normal procedure, though the van didn't have any particular security.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: So then the question to me is well, could somebody have done something to those ballots on the way there?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Could the driver have been in on it? Switched to a different van with fraudulent ballots? It would have been super hard, he tells them. The ballots would have to have been prepared in advance. The identifying numbers on the ballots and the addresses on them would have to match up with real voters who hadn't voted elsewhere.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: And so that's a lot of crazy rigmarole. And in the end, what are they going to gain when they know that in Detroit, these absentee ballots are going to run 95% for Joe Biden?

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: No way.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: They always do.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: No way. They didn't the last election.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Sure they did.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Not 95%.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: The absentee ballots in Detroit?

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Oh, absentee.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: They tend to run very high for the Democrat side. Trump did better than any Republican for 70 years. And so--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Trump won Michigan, the guy said there. Ed told me in the days after the election, he started out with the same questions these two people have. There were lots of calls into his office after the election. And it wasn't like he automatically assumed there was fraud. But there was stuff he definitely felt deserved looking into.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Why am I seeing these news reports of chaos at a polling place? Why am I hearing about late night deliveries? Why did one county here flip so dramatically from one candidate to the other? Why are there rumors of overseas--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It was a long list. Ed thought, well, I can try to figure this stuff out. He heads the Michigan Senate Oversight committee. So he started an investigation.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Anyone who had anything to say could testify. The hearings went on for months. And Ed got way into the details. What if someone was given a Sharpie to mark their ballot and it bled through?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: How does the election management software work? What happens if someone runs a bunch of ballots through the counter twice?

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: That took time for me to learn. And then I had to verify that what I learned was accurate, because you don't want to just take one source as authoritative. I wanted to check others.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It took way longer than he'd thought. He'd run down one theory. But then someone would say, well, what if it happened this way? So he'd look into that.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: As the original ideas started to fall to the wayside, I did begin to grow less and less suspicious that I was going to find anything that was going to overturn the results of the election.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: How much time did you spend looking into it do you think, all told?

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Oh, I don't know. It was hundreds of hours.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Ed put together a 35-page report with a 20-page appendix. He lays out each of the theories and really why they can't be true. When the report came out, both Trump and Obama tweeted about it. Actually, Trump issued a statement, since he'd been banned from Twitter.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Ed says he doesn't imagine either of the former presidents actually read it. Dan and Donna, that's their names, did not seem like they had read it.

segments.speaker: Donna
segments.text: What I want to tell you is that I know you have children. We have seven children. We have 17 grandchildren. And if we don't straighten this out now in 2021-- I don't like Biden. I like Trump. But that has nothing to do with it at all-- our children will never have a free election, if this communism, socialism crap--

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: What is so wrong with an audit?

segments.speaker: Donna
segments.text: Because-- you know, because listen.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Then you could prove Biden won.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: What is the question you started with?

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: And he should be one--

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: That's the question you started with. So for one thing, the state has done two audits.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Not thorough forensic ones like Arizona did.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: So I'll tell you--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Again, Ed goes into all the details. The state had already done a thorough audit, where they recounted a sample of paper ballots by hand from all over the state.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: When we go and recount these precincts by hand, we don't find a single one of them to be out of line. Not one of them is out of line. And we did this audit--

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: So both--

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Actually, a much more substantive audit than just that, because in that audit process, they don't just hand recount the ballots. But they're also checking the signatures. They're checking the applications. They're checking the paperwork for the testing. They're checking the test decks that go in.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Who is doing the checking?

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: So the clerk's office.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: And are they all Democrats?

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: No. All over the state. You have more Republican clerks than you have Democrat clerks all over the state. And most of the counties have multiple parties.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: So you have your county clerk within your townships. You'll have Democrats and Republicans. And so these people are all looking at each other.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: He doesn't seem to be making much headway. The problem Ed runs into all the time is that he'll carefully build this wall out of blocks of facts. But the person he's talking to will just pivot to another claim, which is exactly what happens next.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: I'm just wondering what was wrong with doing a full audit?

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Well, and I'm glad you asked. I mean--

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: I mean, of the machines too.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: And did they change the batteries in the machines?

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: So the machines that they changed the battery in--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The idea here is that the batteries had been changed in some of the voting machines, causing them to erase data. Ed tells them, the machines with the batteries in them were just machines that marked ballots for people with disabilities, not ballot counting machines.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: You sound so calm in a lot of this. Are you feeling calm? You've said these sentences so many times. Is there some part of you that is tired of it?

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: There's a bit of a exhaustion, I suppose. But no. I mean, I feel very-- I don't know if it's compassionate or just passionate about helping people find the truth. I wanted the truth.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: I looked hard. I have resources not every person has because of my position. I used them. Now, I want to give the benefit that I have found to other people.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I feel like that's the perfect answer. I guess I'm asking if you actually always feel that way?

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: I would say 99% of the time.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Ed's been talking to this couple for about 25 minutes at this point. He doesn't seem to be moving them. But again, this is his strategy, answer every question they have.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Then something happens though that throws a wrench in this whole thing. By now, a small crowd of people has gathered around. And one guy who's been watching jumps in. His first word-- baloney.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: --have proved themselves less than trustworthy.

segments.speaker: Man 1
segments.text: Baloney.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: He tells Ed he doesn't understand why they can't have an independent audit. He's pretty insistent.

segments.speaker: Man 1
segments.text: Audits should be done for everything.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: We've don a very substantial audit.

segments.speaker: Man 1
segments.text: We counted the same garbage that was there in the first place. OK, why were the elections in six states closed off at 3:00 in the morning and only to resume at 8:00, when that's never happened before?

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: It didn't happen in Michigan.

segments.speaker: Man 1
segments.text: It certainly did in Michigan.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Absolutely did not. That's a lie. People are lying to you. It didn't happen.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Now Ed says, it's no longer just him having a conversation with this couple. It's like a live version of what happens on social media, and I think why things go so badly there. Ed's trying to have one conversation, and feels like he's maybe getting somewhere. And then this disruptor comes in from the side.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: And you still had Democrat and Republican poll workers there the whole time.

segments.speaker: Man 1
segments.text: Sounds like you convinced yourself, but I know what I saw. I can't get past the fact that there's no fraud to be seen. Really, Ed?

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: I didn't say that. The report doesn't--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Ed later learned that this guy-- he's the son of the couple who was talking to Ed. Ed doesn't convince any of them. Dan, the dad who'd come up with his wife at the beginning, who Ed hoped to make headway with said he just didn't think Ed had the expertise to evaluate the election. And what are you going to say to that?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: A whole half hour of careful effort on Ed's part to lead them down a logical path is undercut in a sentence. He's trying, Dan said, I'll give him that. He's trying his best.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I watched Ed talk to one more woman. She came up after the others have gone. She was middle aged and full of questions. She brought up almost an exact list of things the others did-- the van in the middle of the night, dead people voting, whether the voting machines could have been hacked.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: You're saying the modems, or the computers were not connected to the internet?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The conversation feels like it's going exactly like the other conversation. They talk about the hacking possibility for a long time. But then they talk about Afghanistan and the price of electricity in the Upper Peninsula, which they agree on. It's expensive.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This time, they don't get interrupted by anyone else. It's just two people talking at the state fair, which I think maybe more than Ed's laying out all the facts, is the reason why this might work. If he can put in enough time with someone, be with them long enough, they get a sense for him. There's a power in physically being in the same space as another person. They're real in a way that someone online or on TV isn't.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Finally, they circle back to the election from so many months ago. Here's how the conversation ends.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: If something comes up, I hope you will support an audit, forensic audit.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: To look for any new compelling issue that we can't answer with the information we have-- I'm all ears to hear it. I'm curious too. I want answers.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: But all the issues they bring forward are either flagrantly impossible or issues that have already dealt with to a deep dive extent. And I just keep on asking them, show me where I'm wrong. And rather than do that, they just call me names or say I'm a bad person or paid off by China and shoot the messenger. And I'm like, please, shoot the message for me, because that would help me then go forward and find out what I did wrong.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: But I don't-- they don't do that. And it's frustrating because I'm just as curious as you are about it.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: Just in talking to you and getting the opposite, you know--

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: I appreciate you giving us an open ear to it. And certainly, if you have other questions, you hear something else, just call, message me, call the office.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: Certainly. Well, it's good to hear from you.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Thank you. Thanks for your time.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: Yep.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Can I ask, did it-- does it change anything for you?

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: I'm going to go back and reread several things and re-listen to a few podcasts and stuff, and just--

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: I hope you'll look up the report.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: Yeah, I think I will.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: I'd appreciate it.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: Yeah. Like you said, it's 58 pages. So I'll have to take the time.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It was the furthest I saw him get that day.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Ed tells me he has seen people change their minds. But usually, he learns it because they come back to him later, sometimes with follow-up questions. He wasn't surprised nobody switched sides right in front of us.

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: You can't expect anybody to just disregard their long-held viewpoint or the narrative that they've accepted as being true. You can't expect them on the spot to really discard that. They need time to think.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I pointed out that according to that national poll from earlier in the summer, something like 2/3 of Republicans, or people who lean Republican, believe Biden only won because of voter fraud. Ed says in his experience, it's fewer. But he humors me.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Can we do the math for a second?

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: How many people are in your Senate district?

segments.speaker: Ed McBroom
segments.text: Oh, around 270-ish, I would say.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: Dad, what? I get off the phone and remember, I had done a 23andMe a few years back. So I go to the site. Suddenly, I'm on a side project of proving my father is actually my father. And I click a link I'd never seen before-- view all DNA relatives.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: And Ernie the Attorney's face pops up off the screen again, along with his three kids identified as my half nieces and nephew. I have no idea why confirming Ernest as my brother confirms my father is my father, but it just does. The question now is, do we contact this sweet-looking, innocent 62-year-old man and overturn everything he believes about his identity?

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: We decide to go for it. And I email him saying, I believe you're my half brother. And then Liz and I act like crazy people for the next 24 hours until he emails back. And the next day, we're meeting for the first time on Zoom.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: He tells us that his parents got divorced when he was five and there was a big custody battle. And when he was 17, his mother, in a fit of boozy despair, blurted out that his father was not his father, that his father was a man named Stephen Darst, who is a writer from St. Louis.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: And then Ernest, raised by a psychoanalyst, says he considered the information and had no idea what to do with it, and promptly repressed it. And no one ever talked about it after that day. He says he never thought of it again until I emailed him.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: One weird coincidence, he tells us that for years, his father dated a woman who lived in Bronxville, New York. And they would go visit her all the time in Bronxville, where we lived. We could have run into him at the A&P.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: The following week, Liz goes to my dad's and helps him get on a Zoom with everybody. And suddenly, I'm watching my 87-year-old father meet his 62-year-old son. And I'm seeing Ernie get information about his mother from my dad, who remembers absolutely every detail about everything-- the restaurants they went to, how she called her dog Daisy "Desi" in her accent, how every time they would part they would walk about 100 feet in opposite directions, and my father would turn around and yell, hey, Raqui.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: And when she turned around, my dad would make this embracing gesture with his arms. Earnest says to me, it's amazing to talk about my mom with a man who loved her, which Swedish dad did not. Ernie sends us pictures of Raqui. She looks like a Panamanian Sophia Loren. In fact, Raqui was a lot like my mom. She was beautiful, sort of fancy. Her grandfather was the president of Panama.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: She drank too much, smoked too much, and had major depression. My dad definitely has a type. The whole thing with Ernie was fun and exciting. My sisters and I were talking on the phone all the time, you know, the three of us that are currently speaking to each other.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: But also what made it so exciting was how together an "adulty" he was. He sent me a card with a watercolor drawing of his house in New Orleans on the front, which when I got it, I was like, oh, my God, he's got stationery. None of us girls have stationery.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: He's decent and caring and even-tempered. He asks me how I am and how I feel about this or that. And then he waits for me to answer.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: He made me Raqui's Panamanian Christmas cookies. He was kind, not something in great supply in my showboating drinking, dancy family. Kind is what my mother would have said about people who couldn't throw a decent cocktail party. People who just weren't with it.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: I started to feel like this was our chance to be a bona fide loving family. So Liz and I had a plan to throw an 88th birthday party for our dad and lure Ernie and his wife Donna to New York for it. We never actually said this to each other, but the big question in the air was, is this going to be a real relationship? Is this just going to be a few Zoom calls, or are we going to get together at holidays with our kids for years to come?

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: We'd get together in person and Liz's backyard to find out. You know, no pressure.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: Since Ernie is a lot more normal than we are, after he accepts the invitation to come and meet all of us, Liz and I agree we need to get our curb appeal together, just a light retouching of a few family dramas, just price out some smoke and a few mirrors. I mean, should we say mom died of alcoholism in a West Village [BLEEP] with mice running around? Or should we just say she was a rich girl from St. Louis, who was a champion equestrian and debutante?

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: And do we mention that Amy married a Tunisian man and took off to his family's farm in Tunisia and didn't speak to any of us for eight years but is now back and never really explained any of this to us? The real worry though is, of course, my father. How do we prevent Ernie from seeing that while my father is the ideal person to sit next to at a bar-- funny, a million stories, a truly entertaining charismatic man-- those aren't the most important qualities in a father? He's painfully unaware of other people's needs and feelings.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: And when you really do need him, he's just not able to be there for you in the way that you want him to be. Like, when my mother died of a stroke after years of really grim alcoholism, he offered no words of comfort, but instead asked me what we should do with the bloody couch that she died on. Should I go over to mama's and take that bloody couch out of view so you girls don't have to see it? Although, where the hell am I going to drag a bloody couch? I'll probably get arrested.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: Is seeing that bloody couch going to traumatize you girls, do you think? When I tried to get him to talk about what he was feeling or take some interest in what I was feeling, he wasn't mean about it. He's not a mean person. It's more like he just can't do it, like he'd gently reroute the conversation in a different direction.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: Get him on the phone, and within two minutes, he launches into a steroid-fueled monologue about his obsession with the beginnings of the neocon movement or with Russian ballerina Diana Vishneyva. And once he's off and running, there's no interrupting him. You just wander in and out of the room with him on speaker, doing your laundry, making dinner, because he can go on forever. You just have to make a decision about when you can no longer go on.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: And so I guess I'm worried about Ernie's big day. The day of the party was extremely humid and buggy in my sister's backyard in Brooklyn. And rain threatened to force us inside, where it would be very cramped.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: Seeing my father next to Ernie for the first time was mind-bending they looked so much alike. After some hugs and pictures, we all sit at the long outside table. I'm welling up. I can't imagine how emotional this must be for Ernie. His wife Donna is squeezing his hand in support.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: I look around the table and wonder, why is Ernie not sitting next to my dad? Shouldn't my dad have said, Ernie, sit next to me? It's like he forgets he's the dad.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: But very quickly, we all get talking and laughing. And Ernie gives my dad a picture of Raqui for his birthday. And it feels like the whole thing is going great. Then the rain comes down, and we hustle inside, and we're fumbling to get back to that initial connection.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: Then the rain stops. And we're back in the yard, eating, drinking. Down the table, I see my father, now sitting next to Ernie. But Ernie hasn't said anything for a really long time. So I know my dad is definitely talking about F. Scott Fitzgerald and his theory that Fitzgerald forced his wife Zelda to have an abortion at the Plaza Hotel in 1922, a topic which has dominated our lives for decades. For as long as I can remember, it's the number one thing he uses to avoid talking about anything real.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: When my son was four weeks old, and my husband and I were about to move to California, he said he was stopping by with a present for the baby, which turned out to be some Stilton from Murray's Cheese shop. And as I hobbled around post c-section, packing our suitcases and breastfeeding the baby, completely about to fall apart, he nibbled on the blue cheese and talked about Zelda Fitzgerald's abortion and its aftermath.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: Liz and I had strategized before the party that if he got on Fitzgerald, we would cut him off before it could get going. But it's too late now. I'm horrified, because I don't think my dad has asked Ernie anything about him.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: Does he honestly have zero curiosity about this person, this child whom he almost missed entirely? Ernie looks bewildered and heartbroken. Watching a 62-year-old man get crushed right in front of me, watching him wait patiently to be seen by a man whose eyes are looking elsewhere, it was like watching my spirit get crushed, like a reenactment.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: My father produces a fountain pen that Raqui gave him. It's engraved with his initials. Ernest looks really excited. But my father isn't saying, this is for you Ernest. I want you to have this.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: We all wait for him to say that. But instead, he says, now, should I hang on to this and give it to you later or now? I yell, now, Dad. The metal tip is slightly bent. It doesn't work. But you have to hand it to my dad for simply not losing it for over half a century.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: He gives it to Ernie. Ernie looks thrilled and says, I know a guy in New Orleans who can fix it.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: In my post-mortem with my dad a few days later, he talks about the food, about my niece's pretty dress, talks about all kinds of things. But I have to push him really hard to say anything about meeting his son. I'm practically mugging him for an emotion.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: Finally he says, I think I'll have a great relationship with Ernie. And I thank you very much for that, Jean-Joe, for bringing us together. So much for my dream of Ernie transforming us into a more loving family.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: Let's be honest. My family is like a long-running production of The Fantasticks, where all the actors are too old for the characters they're playing and the lighting people miss a third of the cues. But now, there's this one fresh faced kid just out of drama school who brings down the house in every scene.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: Ernie sends an email after the party where he describes our family as, having a bond I truly admire, and that he felt included in a way that felt genuine and from the heart. Wow, Liz says, we really put on a hell of a show. And then Liz and I have a Zoom with Ernie, Ernest, Ernest Enrique Svenson.

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: Steve sent me something after the weekend, he says. What, we ask? 117 page transcript of Zelda and F. Scott's therapy sessions that Steve hand copied at the Princeton archives. Have you seen it, he asks?

segments.speaker: Jeanne Darst
segments.text: Oh, Ernie, have we seen it? Yes, we have, we say, not sure how much to give away. He's got a long road ahead. And he's got to walk it just like we did. It's pretty interesting, Ernie says. Yeah, we say, yeah, it is.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jeanne Darst, she's currently developing her book, Fiction Ruined My Family for television.
